reason: The elite figures in this text—Shechem (described as 'nesi'a ha'aretz,' the prince/ruler) and his father Hamor—are portrayed unfavorably overall. Shechem initiates the narrative with a violent act: he forcibly takes Dinah and lies with her, which is explicitly labeled as a 'nevala' (abomination) by Jacob's sons. While the text acknowledges Shechem's subsequent affection for Dinah and his desire to marry her, as well as Hamor's reasonable attempts to negotiate intermarriage, these elements do not redeem the initial transgression. Both elite figures are ultimately portrayed as agents of harm who are punished by death. Even their attempts at reparation and negotiation do not alter their fundamental culpability or the negative arc of their portrayal. Jacob himself rebukes the situation as troubling to his household, reinforcing the unfavorable assessment of the elite characters' actions.
